analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal provision that lets states bar mandatory union fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then a subcommittee, and received no hearing or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal labor law currently lets states pass 'right-to-work' laws that bar union contracts requiring workers who benefit from union representation to pay fees for it. This bill would strike that provision from the National Labor Relations Act, so no state could ban such fees. Supporters say unions would be stronger and better funded; opponents say no worker should be forced to pay a union to keep a job.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in right-to-work states who would have the choice to form or keep union contracts with mandatory dues or fees, since unions would collect more revenue and have more bargaining power. Research generally links union coverage to higher wages for both members and nonmembers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the provision that allows states to prohibit agreements requiring union membership or fees as a condition of employment.
By preempting contrary state law, the bill would let unions and employers negotiate union-security agreements everywhere in the country, ending the patchwork of state right-to-work laws.
With union-security agreements allowed nationwide, unions could collect dues and fees from the workers they represent, giving them more resources for bargaining.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who prefer not to financially support a union would lose the right-to-work option: in workplaces with union-security agreements they could be required to pay dues or fees as a condition of employment. Employers in right-to-work states would lose a source of bargaining leverage and could face higher labor costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers who decline to join unions

drawbacks.text: The bill would override state labor policies in more than half the states, removing from those states the choice they currently have over union-security rules, which opponents frame as a worker-freedom issue rather than a business issue.

Workers who benefit from union bargaining but do not wish to join or fund the union would no longer be able to decline payment, since the bill allows agreements requiring union membership or fees as a condition of employment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tradeoff is genuine: stronger, better-funded unions tend to raise pay and bargaining power for the workers they cover, but the cost falls directly on individual workers who would be required to pay dues or fees to keep a job, and on states that lose control over their own labor rules. The bill did not attempt a middle path such as permitting fee-only agreements without full membership, so it asks skeptics to accept the strongest version of union security.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to its health, employment, labor, and pensions subcommittee, and died there with no hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Brad Sherman introduced the bill on July 14, 2016, with 48 original cosponsors, all of them Democrats.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On September 19, 2016, it was referred to the subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action was recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, employers and workers opposed to mandatory union fees kept the status quo: state right-to-work laws remain in force and unions gained nothing.

for.name: Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, Republican-controlled in the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed there until the Congress ended.

against.name: John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a hearing or vote during the 114th Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 19, 2016, and took no recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would let unions negotiate agreements requiring workers they represent to pay dues or fees, significantly increasing union revenue and bargaining resources. Broader union coverage is generally associated with higher pay for the workers affected, which is why supporters saw union and worker interests as aligned here.

Repealing Section 14(b) would end state right-to-work protections employers can currently rely on, exposing them to union-security agreements and potentially higher labor costs. Their preference for keeping right-to-work rules runs against the interests of workers seeking stronger union bargaining power.
